extracted.intended_audience: scientists, researchers, and educated readers of Nature (early-20th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of evaluative criteria and standards used in Nature's editorial and book-review pieces for assessing scientific reports, books, and state research organisation. Focuses on qualities such as clarity, evidence, arrangement, scope, methodology, and policy recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of verbatim reports from researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: A report or Blue-book is improved by containing verbatim reports from Directors of Research who do not disdain, on occasion, the aid of the poets in describing their labours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of authentic, first-hand accounts (even literary ones) adds interest and value to official reports; such verbatim material makes a Blue-book unusually interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for both 'free' and 'directed' research in state organisation
rubrics_metrics.description: State organisation of research should provide for (1) 'free' research concerned with fundamental problems and (2) 'directed' research devoted to definite economic problems, with no attempt to lay down a definite border line between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both kinds of research are necessary; an Advisory Committee of scientific men should control both and the Commissioners should accept its advice unhesitatingly. This balance is presented as one of the best forms of organisation for fishery investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory committee composition and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of research activities should rest with an Advisory Committee composed of scientific men whose advice is accepted by Commissioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and funding decisions are better informed when guided by a committee with strong scientific representation; acceptance of its advice is recommended as good practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate detailed review to economically important topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports should devote substantial, detailed sections to the progress made in solving problems of high economic and social importance (example: fishery research given a large detailed review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an industry (e.g., British sea fisheries providing ~13 million tons annually) is of great national importance, the report should provide thorough analysis, examples, and empirical findings (e.g., migration studies, purification methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, well-informed, well-arranged, well-written treatment (technical books)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good industry or technical book should be 'concise and well-informed', 'well arranged and well written', with a rational classification that conduces to logical treatment of the subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite space limitations, the work should deal in sufficient detail with important phases, be divided into logical parts and subsections, and present terminology, history, chemistry, occurrence, manufacture, and testing in appropriate sections (example: the nine-part structure used for petroleum topics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and sufficiency of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewer values treatment that, given stated limitations (e.g., space), nonetheless covers the subject's most important phases in sufficient detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books should balance breadth and depth: include essential processes (drilling, distillation, cracking), product uses, and methods of testing/standardising, while recognising limits of a concise volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound knowledge and balanced judgment in historical synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: A survey history should be based on sound knowledge and appreciation of historical fact, avoiding over-emphasis on externals and picturesque figures at the expense of deeper spiritual or intellectual factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons across eras must rest on accurate estimation of contributions (e.g., Rome's legal work, medieval Church). The historian should not omit major constructive influences (philosophy, science) and should avoid superficiality and unjustified judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting faults of judgment and proportion; coverage of key figures/events
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful short history should correct previous faults of judgment and proportion, give adequate space to significant figures and movements (e.g., include Dante, Descartes when relevant), and maintain proportion in treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omissions of important figures or intellectual themes are blemishes; an introductory volume must still integrate philosophy and spiritual/intellectual threads when treating religion and wider civilisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific rigour: avoid broad generalisations; verify and document data
rubrics_metrics.description: Works in natural history or biology should show scientific spirit, be 'chary of broad generalisations', and take pains to collect and verify information, since in some cases beginnings and stages can be dated and traced (example: introductions in New Zealand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid sweeping claims (e.g., permanent changes in species) without minute examination and should acknowledge limits imposed by time-scale and available evidence. Systematic cataloguing and verification enhance the work's lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic classification and comprehensive cataloguing
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper plan is to consider each introduced species in its systematic order and to provide measured, dated stages of progress when possible; such systematic treatment makes the work a standard contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise material simply but rigorously (introduction, historical review, then species-by-species systematic treatment). Careful cataloguing of mammals, birds, and plants with establishment status is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation: require advisory committee with biological representation for introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalisation (introducing exotic animals/plants) should not be permitted except with the consent of a properly constituted advisory committee containing a strong representation of biological science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions with ecological consequences must be informed by biological expertise to avoid harmful or irreversible effects; anecdotal enthusiasm is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of exposition, logical argument, and justification of inductive reasoning (philosophical/scientific works)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical or theoretical scientific works should expound hypotheses with admirable clearness, explain inductive proofs and why their inductive arguments are valid, and exhibit clear ideas of continuity, impenetrability, and progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should carefully explain their a priori arguments while remaining in touch with empirical science; clarity of thought and precise exposition of laws are highlighted as virtues (example: Boscovich's acceleration-law exposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority derived from handling authentic examples and high-quality illustrations (art/history books)
rubrics_metrics.description: Handbooks on material culture (e.g., porcelain) should proceed from curators or experts with access to large authentic collections; they should set forth manufacture, decoration motives, and be richly and excellently illustrated to serve as standard authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous, varied, and excellent illustrations (colour and half-tone) coupled with knowledge from handling authentic pieces strengthen a work's lasting value and attract public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness, comprehensive coverage, and supporting scholarship (medical texts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A medical/surgical text should give an admirable account of present knowledge and practice, include historical background, fully consider donor selection and techniques (e.g., sodium citrate method), and supply a substantial bibliography and good index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical preference and technique should be clearly described for practitioners; shortcomings include insufficient discussion of experimental foundations or of unanswered biological questions (e.g., fate and lifespan of transfused red cells).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be evidence-based; avoid unsupported theories (phonation example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must support unusual or counterintuitive claims with evidence; misleading assertions (e.g., that the human voice is produced by frontal sinuses and not vocal cords) are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers/ authors should be teachable and rely on established experimental observations and modern techniques (laryngo-stroboscopic photography, kinematograph) and cite up-to-date specialist literature when making physiological claims.
